subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Who Lives Near Plants? — Recognising Twelve Animals
periods.textbook_anchor: Plants and Animals Live Together — Students discuss which animals from the visual spread on page 63 they have seen before, describing where and how big they are (p. 64)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook page 63 visual spread of twelve animals

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens the class by asking: 'Have you ever sat under a tree and noticed who else was there?' Students share freely. The teacher then directs everyone to open Textbook p. 63 and look at the full spread of animals quietly for a moment.

Class discussion: students point to animals on Textbook p. 64 they have personally seen — frog, tailorbird, squirrels, ants, caterpillar, butterfly, woodpecker, moth, barbet, stink bug, earthworms, elephants — and say where they saw each one. Students use their fingers, hands, and arms to show how small or big each animal is, making the size comparison physical and memorable.

The teacher reads aloud the 'Do you know?' panel with students following along. After each animal mentioned — owl, camel, crow, monkey, sunbird, tailorbird, bat, leopard, caterpillar — the class discusses: what does this animal get from the plant? Students distinguish food, shelter, and nesting uses.

Students identify which of the twelve animals live underground. The teacher closes with the open question: 'Why do you think animals need to stay near plants?' — inviting three or four quick oral responses, leaving the question open for personal wondering rather than a fixed answer.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify animals in their immediate environment and describe where and how they have personally encountered them.
periods.section_context: Twelve animals shown in relation to plant parts: frog, tailorbird, elephants, squirrels, ants, caterpillar, butterfly, woodpecker, moth, barbet, stink bug, earthworms; 'Do you know?' panel on camels, owls, crows, monkeys, sunbirds, bats, leopards.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen an animal living inside a plant — not just near it?' This draws out the hollow, nest, and underground examples naturally. Give quieter children a turn by asking them to show the size with their hands even if they cannot yet say where they saw the animal.

periods.activity_title: Why Animals Choose Plants — Connecting Need to Place
periods.textbook_anchor: Plants and Animals Live Together — Students find out why animals choose to live near plants (p. 64)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the inquiry question from Textbook p. 64: 'Why do these animals choose to live near plants?' Students think silently, then share in pairs before speaking to the class. The teacher lists three broad headings on the board: Food — Shelter — Rearing young.

Class discussion in which students place each animal they remember from the visual spread under one or more headings. The teacher probes: 'Does the squirrel come only for food, or for something else too?' and 'What would happen to the tailorbird if there were no leaves?' Students build the understanding that most animals depend on plants for more than one need.

Students open their notebooks and draw a simple three-column table headed Food / Shelter / Rearing young. They write or draw at least four animals in the correct column(s), working individually. The teacher circulates and asks each child to read one entry aloud quietly.

Sharing round: two or three students read their favourite entry and explain their reasoning. The teacher concludes by naming the idea — plants and animals need each other — without prescribing further answers, keeping curiosity open.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain, using examples, why animals choose to live near plants by linking animal needs to what plants provide.
periods.section_context: Animal needs met by plants: food (leaves, nectar, fruits), shelter (tree hollows, branches, leaf nests), rearing young (twigs for nests, stitched leaves); animals including owl, camel, crow, monkey, sunbird, tailorbird, bat, caterpillar.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of a plant near your home where you have seen an animal? What was the animal doing there?' This draws on children's own neighbourhood observations. Accept region-specific animals children mention — a mango tree with a koel, a banyan with bats — as equally valid.

periods.activity_title: Handful of Soil — A Sensory Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students pick up a little soil near their plant friend, observe how it looks and feels, note moisture, smell it, and find leaves or insects in it (p. 64)
materials: Access to a patch of soil near a plant in the school grounds

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the idea that soil is not just dirt but a living mixture — broken rock, old leaves, roots, and tiny creatures. Students read the opening of the Life in the Soil section together, with the teacher pointing to Textbook p. 64.

The class moves to the school garden or a patch of soil near a plant. Following the prompt on Textbook p. 64, each student picks up a small amount of soil with both hands. They examine colour, texture (rough, smooth, hard, grainy), moisture (dry or damp), and any visible leaves or insects. Students smell the soil and try to remember the smell. The teacher circulates with prompts: 'Press it — does it hold together or crumble?'

Back in the classroom, students record their observations in a three-row table: What I saw / What I felt / What I smelled. They note whether they found any insects or leaf pieces. The teacher asks each pair to compare notes: did the soil from different spots feel the same?

Brief class share: which properties came up most often? The teacher introduces the names of common soil creatures — ants, termites, beetles — and asks: 'Why do you think these tiny animals live in the soil near plants and not somewhere else?' Students offer ideas freely; the teacher does not resolve the question but notes it on the board for continued wondering.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured sensory investigation of a natural material, recording observations of appearance, texture, moisture, and smell in an organised way.
periods.section_context: Soil near a plant: colour, texture (rough, smooth, hard, grainy), moisture (dry, damp), smell, presence of leaves and insects; soil creatures including ants, termites, beetles.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone smelled soil after rain? How was it different?' This surfaces seasonal knowledge and intergenerational observation children may have learned from elders at home. Allow students who are hesitant to touch soil to use a stick or leaf to examine it — full participation matters more than method.

periods.activity_title: Soil Near and Far — Comparing Two Samples
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students stand near their plant friend, look around, spot as many different animals as they can, and fill in the observation table (p. 66)
materials: Two small containers or folded paper envelopes (one labelled 'near plant', one labelled 'away from plant')
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 66 observation table and animal pictures

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets up the comparison question: does soil under a plant differ from soil in an open area with no plants? Students predict in pairs, then share. The teacher notes three or four predictions on the board without evaluating them.

In pairs, students collect two small samples — one from near a plant, one from open ground — in their envelopes or containers. They open Textbook p. 66 and, standing near their plant friend, observe and count every different animal, bird, or insect they can spot. They record names or descriptions (colour, size, shape) in the table on Textbook p. 66, using the provided pictures as a reference.

Back in the classroom, students compare their two soil samples side by side: colour, texture, any creatures or leaf matter. They record differences in their notebook. The teacher asks: 'Which sample had more living things in it? Why might that be?'

Class discussion: students report their animal counts from near the plant versus what they expected to find in open ground. The teacher connects observations to the chapter's core idea — soil near plants is richer in living things — and invites children to wonder about what the animals are finding there.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare two natural samples by recording observable differences in appearance, texture, and the presence of living organisms.
periods.section_context: Soil near a plant versus soil away from plants: colour, texture, moisture, presence of living organisms; animals spotted near plant friend recorded in observation table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'At home, have you seen more insects under a bush or in an open dusty patch?' This draws on everyday neighbourhood experience. If two samples look very similar, prompt students to compare smell and moisture rather than giving up — multiple properties matter.

periods.activity_title: Monsoon Arrivals — Where Do New Plants and Animals Come From?
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students discuss where new plants and animals come from in the monsoon and why they could not be seen earlier (p. 66)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a memory prompt: 'Think of a place you pass every day — a garden wall, a roadside patch, your school compound. Does it look different after heavy rains?' Students share observations. The teacher then poses the textbook question from p. 66: 'In the monsoons, you may find many more plants and animals around. Where did these new plants and animals come from?'

Small-group discussion (groups of three or four): students brainstorm why so many plants and animals appear in monsoon that were invisible before. Groups consider seeds waiting in soil, animals hiding underground, creatures arriving from nearby areas. Each group nominates one idea to share. The teacher records all ideas on the board as a list without judging any.

The teacher guides a class discussion connecting the groups' ideas to the science in the chapter: seeds germinate when moisture arrives; earthworms and millipedes come to the surface after rain; insects that were dormant or in other stages become active. Students add one new thing they learned to their notebook as a short sentence or drawing.

The teacher raises the question of seasonal knowledge: 'Do people in your family know which month certain birds or insects appear? How do they know?' Students share what elders or family members have said about seasonal changes. The teacher acknowledges that careful watching over many seasons builds this knowledge — connecting human observation to the natural pattern.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain seasonal changes in plant and animal presence by connecting environmental conditions to the emergence or disappearance of living organisms.
periods.section_context: Monsoon emergence of new plants and animals: seeds germinating, earthworms and millipedes surfacing after rain, insects becoming active; seasonal and intergenerational knowledge of seasonal rhythms.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen the ground crack open with tiny plants after the first rain? Where do those plants come from?' This surfaces the seed-dormancy idea naturally. Invite children to share what grandparents or neighbours have told them about which rains bring which animals — this intergenerational knowledge is as valid as textbook knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Birds — Cupped Ears and Sound Records
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students close their eyes, listen for bird sounds, cup their ears to localise the sound, try to imitate bird calls, and record the sounds in the table (p. 68)
materials: Notebook or the textbook sound table

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the listening activity from Textbook p. 68: students will close their eyes, stay still, and try to hear any bird sounds. The class first practises one minute of silence in the classroom to notice what they can hear with eyes closed.

The class moves to a spot outdoors (or opens windows if the school is near trees). Following the textbook activity on p. 68, students close their eyes and listen. They then cup their ears with both hands and point their faces toward a sound — does the sound become louder or clearer? Students try to recognise which bird might be making each sound and try to imitate it softly.

Back in the classroom, students fill in the sound table on Textbook p. 68: name of bird (or description if unknown), description of sound, and time of day heard. The teacher asks: 'Did you hear more sounds in the early morning, afternoon, or evening?' Students discuss and note their answers.

Class shares: two or three students demonstrate the bird sound they heard by imitating it. The teacher asks: 'If you heard no bird sounds at all, what might be the reason?' Students suggest reasons — no trees nearby, noise pollution, wrong time of day. The teacher affirms all reasonable ideas and connects animal sound to the idea of animals living near plants.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use focused listening and directional awareness to detect, locate, and record sounds from living organisms in their environment.
periods.section_context: Bird sound activity: closing eyes to listen, cupping ears to localise sound direction, imitating bird calls, recording bird names and sound descriptions in a table at different times of day.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do the birds you hear near a leafy tree sound different from birds near an empty building?' This helps children notice that richer plant environments attract more bird sound. If no bird sounds are audible, treat the silence itself as data — ask children what this tells us about the school environment.

periods.activity_title: Describing Animals Near Plants — Writing and Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students fill in the table describing two animals observed near or on plants — shape, size, colour, and why they were near the plant — then draw their plant friend with coloured dots marking where animals were spotted (p. 70)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pp. 70–71 reflection table and drawing prompt

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens the reflection section on Textbook p. 70 and reads the discussion prompts aloud: What colour and texture was your soil? When did new leaves appear on your plant? Which animals, birds, and insects did you notice? Students discuss in pairs for a few minutes, recalling what they have observed.

Students work individually to fill in the structured table on Textbook p. 70 describing two animals they observed near or on plants. For each animal they write: shape, size, colour, and their best guess as to why the animal was near the plant. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'What shape are its legs?' and 'Was it bigger or smaller than your palm?'

Students turn to Textbook p. 71 and draw their plant friend as they remember or imagine it. Using different coloured small dots, they mark the places on the drawing where they spotted animals, birds, or insects — one colour per type if they wish. They label each dot if they can name the animal.

Quick gallery share: three or four students hold up their drawings and point to where their dots are. The teacher comments on the variety of locations — high up, underground, on leaves — as evidence that a plant is home to many creatures.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations of living organisms through structured written description and annotated drawing, showing shape, size, colour, and location.
periods.section_context: Two animals observed near plants: shape, size, colour, reason for being near plant; annotated drawing of plant friend with coloured dots marking animal locations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you put a dot somewhere on your drawing that is underground? What might live there?' This stretches the drawing to include soil-dwelling creatures children may not have illustrated. Accept any plant — real or imagined — as a valid plant friend if a child has not had outdoor observation time.

periods.activity_title: The Caterpillar's Journey — Sequencing a Life Cycle with an Elder's Help
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students consult an elder person and arrange the stages of a caterpillar's life cycle in order: caterpillar, cocoon, butterfly stages (p. 71)
materials: Scissors (optional — if stages are to be cut out)
Notebook or loose paper for sequencing strips
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 71 life-cycle stages of Suma's caterpillar story

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the story of Suma and the caterpillar from Textbook p. 71 aloud, with students following along. The five jumbled stages are then written on the board in random order. The teacher asks: 'Has anyone watched a caterpillar change? Has an elder in your family ever shown you a cocoon?'

Students work in small groups to arrange the five stages in the correct order, discussing their reasoning. The teacher frames this as a task that benefits from asking someone older who may have watched this happen in a garden or field. Groups record their sequence in notebooks. The teacher circulates and asks each group: 'How do you know that stage comes before this one?'

Class comparison: groups share their sequences. The teacher guides the class to agree on the correct order — caterpillar eats and grows, one day stops eating, forms a cocoon, comes out of the cocoon, becomes a butterfly that flies away — connecting each stage to what the animal needs from its plant environment. Students write the final agreed sequence in their notebooks.

Reflection round: the teacher asks each student to silently think of one thing in nature they would like to watch change over time — a seed, an egg, a bud. One or two students share. The teacher closes with the disposition: careful watching, over time and across generations, is how people have always come to know the natural world.

periods.implied_lo: Students can sequence the stages of an animal life cycle in correct order and explain the change from one stage to the next.
periods.section_context: Caterpillar life cycle stages: caterpillar eating, stopping eating, forming a cocoon, emerging from cocoon, becoming a butterfly that flies away; intergenerational knowledge (consulting an elder).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Who in your family has seen a caterpillar become a butterfly? What did they tell you?' This surfaces intergenerational nature knowledge as a valued source. If groups cannot agree on the order, ask them to justify each step rather than telling them — productive disagreement deepens understanding.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya saw a tailorbird carrying a long thread near a tree. What was the tailorbird most likely using the plant for?

options.label: A
options.text: To drink nectar from the flowers

options.label: B
options.text: To find food like fruits and seeds

options.label: C
options.text: To hide underground away from rain

options.label: D
options.text: To stitch leaves together and make a nest for its young

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether students can connect a specific animal behaviour to the need it fulfils, which was the focus of the identification and discussion activity for this unit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify animals in their immediate environment and describe where and how they have personally encountered them.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the tailorbird with fruit- or seed-eating birds; the student has not distinguished between the food and shelter functions of plants for different animals.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the tailorbird with nectar-drinking animals such as sunbirds and butterflies; the student has not retained which animal uses which plant part.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses above-ground nesters with underground-dwelling animals; the student has not recalled that earthworms and insects — not birds — live underground.

assessment_items.question_text: Rohan noticed that owls live in tree hollows, squirrels use twigs, and sunbirds drink nectar. Choose any two of these animals and explain what need each one is getting from the plant.
expected_elements: Names two animals from the chapter (owl, squirrel, sunbird, or any other chapter example).
States the specific plant part or product each animal uses (hollow, twigs, nectar, leaves, fruits, etc.).
Identifies the need being met for each animal — shelter, nest-building material, or food.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit when both animals are named, the plant part is identified, and the need is stated. Partial credit when one animal is fully explained. Accept region-specific birds or animals children mention if the need-plant connection is correctly described.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain, using examples, why animals choose to live near plants by linking animal needs to what plants provide.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

expected_elements: Names two animals from the chapter (owl, squirrel, sunbird, or any other chapter example).
States the specific plant part or product each animal uses (hollow, twigs, nectar, leaves, fruits, etc.).
Identifies the need being met for each animal — shelter, nest-building material, or food.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena picked up soil near a plant and noticed it felt damp and had some tiny insects in it. She picked up soil from an open patch far from any plant and found it dry and empty. What does this comparison tell us about soil near plants?

options.label: A
options.text: Soil away from plants smells stronger than soil near plants

options.label: B
options.text: Soil near plants has more moisture and living things than soil away from plants

options.label: C
options.text: Soil near plants is always harder and rougher than other soil

options.label: D
options.text: Soil near plants is always red in colour

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item assesses whether students drew the intended conclusion from the sensory soil investigation — that plant-adjacent soil supports more life and retains more moisture.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured sensory investigation of a natural material, recording observations of appearance, texture, moisture, and smell in an organised way.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.D: Overgeneralises one incidental observation (soil colour can vary) into a universal rule; the student has not identified the key comparison outcome.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reverses the expected finding; may reflect a misconception from the smelling activity where open-patch soil was considered 'stronger' because it was dusty.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses texture with moisture; the student may have noted that dry soil feels hard and incorrectly made this the defining feature of plant-adjacent soil.

assessment_items.question_text: Anu collected soil from under a mango tree and from an open sandy patch. She found earthworms and ants in the soil under the tree but nothing in the open patch. Give two reasons why the soil under the tree had more living things.
expected_elements: Mentions that plant-adjacent soil has more moisture, which supports living organisms.
Mentions that fallen leaves, roots, or plant matter in the soil provide food or shelter for insects and worms.
States a connection between the presence of the plant and the conditions that allow creatures to live there (shade, dampness, organic matter — any one accepted).
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any two distinct, valid reasons connecting plant presence to richer soil life. Accept informal language ('the tree keeps it wet', 'leaves fall and the bugs eat them') as long as the causal reasoning is present.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare two natural samples by recording observable differences in appearance, texture, and the presence of living organisms.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

expected_elements: Mentions that plant-adjacent soil has more moisture, which supports living organisms.
Mentions that fallen leaves, roots, or plant matter in the soil provide food or shelter for insects and worms.
States a connection between the presence of the plant and the conditions that allow creatures to live there (shade, dampness, organic matter — any one accepted).

assessment_items.question_text: After the first heavy rains, Kavya noticed that her school garden was suddenly full of new plants and insects that were not there before. Why did this happen? Where were these plants and insects before the rains came?
look_for: Explains that seeds were already present in the soil and germinated when rain brought moisture.
Explains that insects or earthworms were dormant, underground, or in other life stages and became active after rain.
Connects the monsoon condition (moisture, temperature) to the trigger for emergence — not just 'rain came so they appeared'.
Uses at least one specific example from the chapter (earthworms surfacing, millipedes, new shoots, seeds).
Shows understanding that these organisms were present but hidden or inactive, not that they arrived from elsewhere.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response explains both plants (seeds in soil) and animals (dormancy/underground) and connects both to monsoon conditions. A weak response says only 'rain brought them' without explaining where they were before. Award partial credit when only one of the two (plants or animals) is explained with reasoning.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain seasonal changes in plant and animal presence by connecting environmental conditions to the emergence or disappearance of living organisms.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

Explains that insects or earthworms were dormant, underground, or in other life stages and became active after rain.
Connects the monsoon condition (moisture, temperature) to the trigger for emergence — not just 'rain came so they appeared'.
Uses at least one specific example from the chapter (earthworms surfacing, millipedes, new shoots, seeds).
Shows understanding that these organisms were present but hidden or inactive, not that they arrived from elsewhere.

assessment_items.question_text: During a bird-listening activity, students cupped their ears with both hands and pointed toward a sound. What happened when they did this?

options.label: A
options.text: The birds stopped making sounds because the students moved

options.label: B
options.text: They could hear the bird sound more clearly and find its direction

options.label: C
options.text: They could no longer hear any sounds at all

options.label: D
options.text: They could only hear sounds from directly behind them

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item tests recall and understanding of the ear-cupping technique and what it demonstrates about sound localisation, as practised in the listening activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use focused listening and directional awareness to detect, locate, and record sounds from living organisms in their environment.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misunderstands the effect of cupping — the student may have experienced muffling when ears are fully covered and confused cupping outward with blocking.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Attributes a social cause (student movement) to the sound change; the student has not grasped that the change was in their own hearing, not in bird behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the directionality — cupping ears forward amplifies front-facing sounds, not sounds from behind; the student may not have formed a clear spatial model.

assessment_items.task: Think of a plant you have seen — in your school, home, or neighbourhood. Draw this plant. Now use coloured dots or small marks to show where you have seen animals, birds, or insects near or on this plant. Under your drawing, write the name of each animal you marked and one sentence about what it was doing near the plant.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My plant: ___________
Draw your plant here.
(Use different coloured dots or marks to show where you saw animals.)
Animal 1: ___________ — It was near the plant because ___________.
Animal 2: ___________ — It was near the plant because ___________.
format_of_output: Annotated drawing of a plant with coloured dot markers
One sentence per animal describing what it was doing or why it was near the plant
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locally observed plant and any animals the child has genuinely noticed — including common ones such as ants, sparrows, or lizards. Regional variation in plants and animals named is expected and valid. Do not require scientific names. Assess whether the dot placements are purposeful (leaf, branch, soil, hollow) and whether the written reason shows understanding of a need being met.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations of living organisms through structured written description and annotated drawing, showing shape, size, colour, and location.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The task shows whether the student can represent their observation of animal-plant relationships visually and in writing, connecting location to purpose.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold is a guide — students who draw freely and label without the scaffold lines are equally valid. The written sentences are the key evidence of conceptual understanding; the drawing is supporting evidence.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: dots placed in ecologically meaningful spots (underground, on leaf, in hollow), written reasons that reference a need (food, shelter, nesting). Weak: dots placed randomly with no spatial reasoning; written reason is 'the animal was there' with no cause stated.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have not had outdoor observation time may use an imagined or remembered plant from home, a market, or a story. Children with fine-motor difficulty may dictate their labels or use pre-cut animal pictures to stick instead of drawing.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing externalises spatial understanding of where animals live on or near a plant; written labels and sentences make the animal-need connection explicit in language.

assessment_items.task:
Here are five stages in the life of a caterpillar, written in a jumbled order. Cut them out (or copy them) and arrange them in the correct order from first to last. Then, next to each stage, write one sentence saying what the caterpillar or butterfly was doing at that stage.

Stages (jumbled): It flew away gently. | The caterpillar formed a cocoon. | Now it was a butterfly. | One day it stopped eating. | It came out of the cocoon.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Stage 1: ___________ → What was happening: ___________
Stage 2: ___________ → What was happening: ___________
Stage 3: ___________ → What was happening: ___________
Stage 4: ___________ → What was happening: ___________
Stage 5: ___________ → What was happening: ___________
format_of_output: Five stages written or arranged in correct sequence
One explanatory sentence per stage describing what the animal was doing
assessment_items.annotation: The correct sequence is: (1) Caterpillar eats and grows, (2) One day it stopped eating, (3) The caterpillar formed a cocoon, (4) It came out of the cocoon, (5) Now it was a butterfly / It flew away gently. Steps 4 and 5 may be combined or listed in either sub-order. Award full credit for correct sequence with at least three meaningful explanatory sentences. Award partial credit for correct sequence with no explanation, or one or two sequencing errors with good explanatory sentences.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sequence the stages of an animal life cycle in correct order and explain the change from one stage to the next.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The task shows whether the student understands the caterpillar life cycle as an ordered, sequential natural system — not a random set of changes.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold provides slots for each stage and a prompt for explanation. A student who writes the sequence correctly in flowing prose without the scaffold is equally valid.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all five stages in correct order; explanatory sentences that name what is biologically happening at each stage (e.g., 'It stopped eating because it was getting ready to change'). Weak: stages out of order with no explanation; or stages listed correctly but sentences only restate the stage label without explaining the change.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have consulted a family member or elder are demonstrating exactly the intergenerational knowledge the task values — this should be acknowledged positively. Children who cannot write may arrange cut-out slips and explain orally to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Sequential written arrangement with explanatory sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Sequencing makes the life-cycle system visible as a chain of changes; explanatory sentences ensure the student is reasoning about each stage rather than memorising positions.
